confirmed.title: Guard input can overflow max_input_tokens for Llama/OLMo answers; TooLong is uncaught and aborts the checkpoint evaluation
confirmed.defect: The brief's 'Guard input cannot overflow' bound (brief line 116: at most 3.00 Qwen3Guard tokens per policy token, 2,048x3+391+~400<8,192) was derived for the Qwen policy only. The build reuses the same guard section (max_input_tokens 8192, e.g. study-kt-llama31-8b-r64-b-mb4-20261008.json:105) for OLMo and Llama vocabularies without re-establishing the bound. scoring.py:146-148 (score) and 183-185 (label_scores) raise TooLong. Nothing catches it at runner.py:650, 662 or 673, so one long answer aborts the whole checkpoint evaluation.
confirmed.scenario: I measured this with a local script (scratchpad review-mf/guard_ratio*.py): the reference tokenizers plus the cached Qwen3Guard-Gen-4B tokenizer at 6ec42827, vocabulary entries only, no data. The Llama-3 vocab has 1,588 tokens that each re-encode to more than 3.0 Qwen3Guard tokens when repeated, and 47 of them are punctuation runs. Examples: id 125437 '.:.:...' gives 16.0, id 123496 (a run of black circles) gives 16.0, id 121733 (a run of heavy box-drawing lines) gives 8.0. The budget is (8192-391-400)/2048 = 3.61 guard tokens per answer token. So a capped e1 Llama answer that degenerates into about 930 separator tokens at 8 each, or about 470 at 16 each, gives a guard input over 8,192. TooLong is then raised in the 'guard' or 'harm_scores' stage, after that evaluation's generation has already been paid for. The unit has no verdict, so the probe loses its e1 (or init) result. OLMo is lower risk: 0 punctuation-run tokens above 3.6, 40 long-tail tokens up to 5.94, and 14 added non-special tokens at 7-9. Natural text stays low: on my own synthetic sentences in 11 scripts the highest ratio was 2.36 (Greek, Llama), and digits gave 2.2. The likelihood is therefore low but not measured; the cost when it happens is a lost paid probe.
confirmed.fix: The lead should choose one. (a) Record the over-limit case as a counted unscored guard reason ('guard input over limit; not scored') instead of raising, and have family_probe_reading count it next to the control-string unscored answers. Qwen bytes do not change, because the Qwen bound holds. This is an evaluation-rule change, so it needs lead or user approval. (b) If the lead keeps the raise, record it as a known limit in the brief, and add a Mac-side check that prints, per family, the largest Qwen3Guard tokens-per-policy-token over the vocabulary, so the risk is explicit before spend. Raising guard.max_input_tokens would break the 'guard byte-identical to recipe B' rule (I-S2).

- All three token ids the reviewer named are canonical encodings: encoding a run of 16 '●' gives `[123496]`. So the model can plausibly emit them; they are not untrained tokens.

**Vocabulary scan** (`runscan.py`). These are tokens that are one character repeated, measured as guard tokens per policy token:
- Llama-3: 47 tokens are above the 3.61 budget (8,192 minus 391 minus about 400, divided by 2,048). They include:

  - no-break-space runs at 4x (id 115922);

The Qwen policy and the guard both split digits into single tokens, so for Qwen the ratio would be about 1. - The chance is low and has not been measured: it needs a degenerate tail of about 450-930 tokens of a rare formatting token, or nearly the whole answer for the 4x tokens.

CODE PATH, ALL CONFIRMED
- scoring.py:146-148 (score) and 183-185 (label_scores) raise TooLong when the guard input is over max_input_tokens.
- runner.py:650, 662 and 673 call these with no handler. The exception goes to run_one's `except BaseException: _fail(...); raise` at runner.py:335-337, and to eval_state's at runner.py:777-779.
- Both files are byte-identical to the repo. `diff -q` printed nothing, so this is old code used for the new families.
- The guard section in the Llama configs is identical to the Qwen-7B recipe's (dict diff run). max_input_tokens is 8192 (study-kt-llama31-8b-r64-b-mb4-20261008.json:105).
- generation.max_new_tokens is 2048 and model.max_prompt_tokens is 1536 in every family config.
- The checkpoints are q, e1 and e3 (llama32-1b config, train.checkpoints). A raise at q or e1 therefore also loses e3. The policy generation is already paid for when the guard stage runs (runner.py:610-641, before line 650).
- Brief line 116 ("Guard input cannot overflow ... 3.00 tokens per policy token") is the only bound. family_codec_check.py has no guard-ratio check (grep found none).

MY OWN CPU REPRODUCTION
Scripts are in scratchpad review-mf/sk2-guard/. I used the reference tokenizers and the cached Qwen3Guard-Gen-4B and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct tokenizers, with synthetic text only.
1. Guard template overhead is 391 tokens, which matches the brief.
2. A per-vocabulary ratio that ignores reachability reproduces the reviewer's counts: Llama has 1,588 tokens above 3.0 per policy token. But the same method gives Qwen a maximum of 9.0, which contradicts the brief's Qwen bound. So that metric overstates the risk. The fair test is the canonical ratio, guard(s*32)/policy(s*32), counted only when the policy's own tokenizer encodes the repeated run with at most one token per copy.
3. Canonical maxima:
   - Qwen: 1.0.
   - OLMo: 3.0 (3-digit groups). 2048*3+391+400 = 6,935 < 8,192, so OLMo cannot overflow through ordinary vocabulary.
   - OLMo's 14 added non-special tokens are untrained <|extra_id_N|> tokens (7.1-8.1) and the PII placeholders (4.25). The placeholders would have to fill about 1,650 of 2,048 tokens, which is implausible.
   - Llama: 1,537 reachable tokens above 3.61.
4. The reviewer's headline example, id 125437 ('.:.:...'), is not canonical. Llama itself re-encodes that run as 15.9 tokens per copy, so on that text the guard and Llama counts are about equal. The examples 123496 (black circles) and 121733 (heavy box lines) are canonical.
5. End to end through the guard chat template (65-token synthetic prompt), with 2,048 canonical Llama tokens per run, guard input length:

   | Run | Guard input tokens | Over 8,192? |
   |---|---|---|
   | black circle | 33,223 | yes |
   | ideographic space U+3000 | 33,224 | yes |
   | U+045F | 65,992 | yes |
   | heavy box line | 16,841 | yes |
   | no-break space | 8,648 | yes |

   The same runs for OLMo come to 1,480-2,507, all under the limit. The common degeneration runs stay far under for both families: spaces, newlines, tabs, dashes, dots, =, *, _, #, ~, table rows and full blocks give 1,095-2,507. Digits give 6,600.
   At about 16 guard tokens per Llama token, roughly 360-470 such tokens in one capped answer are enough to overflow.

WHY MINOR
- The failure is fail-closed: no wrong verdict is recorded.
- It needs one answer with hundreds of tokens of exotic runs (ideographic space, black circles, U+045F, box lines, no-break spaces). The common greedy loops and the sampled answers (temperature 0.7, 3 per prompt) stay under the limit.
- The cost when it happens is one Llama run. Re-running the same job will probably fail again, because greedy decoding is deterministic and the samples are seeded.

FIX
Fix (b) is enough: record a known Llama limit next to brief line 116, and add a Mac-side canonical-ratio check per family. Fix (a) changes the evaluation rule and needs lead approval. It would leave Qwen and OLMo bytes unchanged, since their canonical ratios are 1.0 and 3.0.

confirmed.title: A failed g16 batch proof (or tokenizer_ok false) does not stop the preflight, and the wrapper re-runs every later candidate
confirmed.defect: The batch proof finishes at cuda_preflight_family.py:358-367, before the guard load. When it fails, the script still runs the guard load, the full-length check, the timed evaluation sample and the BOS record (lines 369-416). The failure only shows up in verdict_of (lines 181-183, 189) as use_this_recipe false. tokenizer_ok is known at line 256 and is handled the same way. The wrapper skips later candidates only after generation_memory_ok false (runkit/family-probe/setup/preflight_probe.py:27-28, 71, 80-81). So a batch-shape (bf16) failure that is close to model-invariant is paid for once per candidate.
confirmed.scenario: olmo2-13b's ladder is all g16 (probes.py, 4 candidates). Batch-vs-single greedy equality over 16 prompts x 256 new tokens (BATCH_PROOF_NEW_TOKENS, line 54) means about 4,096 argmax decisions. The Qwen-7B q7 preflight already showed batch-dependent logits: verdict sampled_batch_equals_single false, sampling same 2 of 3 (tmp/kill-test-7b-check/retrieved/q7-1101/tree/cuda-preflight-2/verification.json). One near-tie flip is therefore likely. If it happens, each of the four 13B candidates runs its whole preflight (model load, memory preflight, a second 13B copy for the untuned comparison, resume check, then about 15-25 min of guard, full-length and sample work). That is about 1.7-4 h of A100 time ($3-6 at $1.59/h) for an ok:false that the first proof already settled, and it can pass preflight_wait_s 9,000 s. olmo2-7b's two g16 fallbacks behave the same way.
confirmed.fix: Exit with a verdict right after the batch proof (and after tokenizer_check) when it fails: write verification.json with batch_proof_ok false (or tokenizer_ok false) and use_this_recipe false, then exit 0, as for memory_ok false. In preflight_probe.py, skip later candidates with the same generation batch and the same attention implementation after batch_proof_ok false, and skip all later candidates after tokenizer_ok false. Also tell the lead that, under decision 4, a likely proof failure means 13B probably cannot run at all.

I tried to refute this and could not. Every code-flow claim holds. The cost figure is overstated, and the finding misses one consequence that matters more than the cost.

**Code flow (all confirmed)**
- The batch proof runs at scripts/cuda_preflight_family.py:356-367. There is no early return after it.
- The script then always runs `session.guard` (line 369), the full-length check and timed sample through `generation_phase` (lines 374-391), and the BOS record (lines 405-416). OLMo-2's template likely starts with BOS, so the BOS record would probably run for these probes too. I did not check the OLMo template locally.
- A failed proof shows up only in `verdict_of` (lines 181-183) and in `use_this_recipe` (line 189).
- `tokenizer_ok` is known at line 256. It never exits early either; it is only copied into the memory-failure verdict (line 265).
- The wrapper skips later candidates only after `generation_memory_ok` false (runkit/family-probe/setup/preflight_probe.py:27-29, 71-73, 80-81). Otherwise it continues to the next candidate (line 84).
- All four 13B candidates use generation batch 16 (runkit/family-probe/probes.py:43).
- The configs differ only in micro_batch/grad_accum and gradient_checkpointing. The last candidate also differs in `attn_implementation` (eager instead of sdpa). I diffed the four configs under experiments/safety_selection/configs/study-kt-olmo2-13b-*.
- `tokenizer_check` (lines 111-130) depends only on the recipe's model and tokenizer pins, which are the same for every candidate of a probe. A false result therefore repeats for every candidate.
- The engine does nothing to make batched and single runs bit-equal (experiments/safety_selection/engine.py:516-545).

**CPU reproduction**
I stubbed `subprocess.run` and the candidate verdicts and ran the real `preflight_probe.main`. The script is in scratchpad/review-mf/wrap_repro.py. Results:
- Proof fails on every candidate: candidates [1, 2, 3, 4] all run, `ok` false.
- `tokenizer_ok` false on every candidate: [1, 2, 3, 4] all run.
- Generation out of memory on the first candidate: only [1] runs.
- Proof fails on candidate 1 and passes on candidate 2: the wrapper picks r2, `ok` true, exit 0.

**Corrections to the finding**
1. **Cost.** The extra cost is three candidates, not four, because the first run is needed anyway. Only candidates that pass the training-memory preflight (line 261) run in full, so mb2-g16 or mb1-g16 may stop after a couple of minutes. The brief estimates about 23 min per passing 13B candidate before the proof was added (brief:416). The proof adds 16 one-at-a-time runs of up to 256 tokens. That gives roughly 30-45 min per extra candidate, about 1-2 h in total, or about $1.6-3.5 at $1.59-1.75/h (host.py:39). The orchestrator also sets an upper limit: after `preflight_wait_s` (9,000 s for 13B), `wait_file` raises (orchestrate.py:90-97, 192-193) and `after_create` stops the pod (orchestrate.py:275-279). The final state is the same pod stop the lead would get from `ok: false`. The difference is that PREFLIGHT-DONE.json and its tried list are never written.
2. **How likely a proof failure is.** The cited Qwen-7B q7 evidence shows only that sampling differed: same 2 of 3. Greedy matched 3 of 3 at 32 tokens (tmp/kill-test-7b-check/retrieved/q7-1101/tree/cuda-preflight-2/verification.json, `generation.same=3`, `n=3`). Greedy flips over 16 prompts × 256 tokens in bf16 are plausible, but this evidence does not establish them.

**Consequence the finding misses**
The proofs on candidates 1-3 run on almost the same weights: the same base model, sdpa attention, and an adapter after only 2 steps. A pass after a fail is therefore partly luck. The wrapper still accepts it: after candidate 1's proof fails, a passing candidate 2 or 3 is chosen. Decision 4 (brief:686) says g16 is allowed "only if the preflight proves" equality, "Otherwise batch 32 and a longer cap." So moving on to the next sdpa g16 candidate after a failed proof goes against that decision, not only against the budget.

**Severity: should-fix.** The proof part is a decision-4 integrity issue, and it only arises on the failure path of a probe the user has not yet approved (decision 6). The `tokenizer_ok` part is a certain repeat once it happens, and the fix is cheap: exit after line 256. The proposed fix is right, including keeping the eager candidate when only an sdpa proof failed.

**Related observation (not part of this finding)**
For olmo2-7b, nothing enforces the brief's rule (brief:346) that its g16 candidates are tried only after a batch-32 candidate records `generation_memory_ok` false. `skipped()` only blocks candidates at or above a failed batch (preflight_probe.py:27-29). If the batch-32 candidates fail for any other reason, the g16 candidates still run.

**Checks**
No workspace file was edited, and no `__pycache__` was left in the workspace runkit.

I tried to refute this finding and could not. The code-path claims hold. Two of the reviewer's numbers are weaker than stated, and there is one consequence the reviewer did not raise.

**What I confirmed (workspace paths)**
- **The script keeps going after a failed proof.** The batch proof runs at scripts/cuda_preflight_family.py:357-367 and only records `report["batch_proof"]`. Nothing between there and the end of the run checks it. Lines 369-416 then run in full: the guard at 369, the full-length check and timed sample through `generation_phase` at 391, `cap_projection` at 402 and the BOS record at 405-416. The failure only shows up in `verdict_of` (176-189): `batch_proof_ok` at 183 and `use_this_recipe` at 189.
- **tokenizer_ok behaves the same way.** It is computed at line 256 and never checked before the verdict.
- **There is a precedent for stopping early.** `memory_ok` false does exit early (260-267), and so does an out-of-memory error while generating (203-212, 391-394).
- **The wrapper only skips on generation_memory_ok false.** See runkit/family-probe/setup/preflight_probe.py:27-29, 71-73 and 80-81. A candidate with `use_this_recipe` false simply moves on to the next one (84-86).
- **CPU reproduction.** I ran a fake-subprocess run of `preflight_probe.main` (scratchpad review-mf/s2-proof/sim.py). It used the real olmo2-13b ladder, with every verdict set to batch_proof_ok false and use_this_recipe false. All 4 candidates ran (generation batches [16,16,16,16]); the run ended ok false with exit 1.
- **The four 13B candidates are nearly the same run.** The ladder is at runkit/family-probe/probes.py:43, and the configs show:

| Candidate | Micro-batch / accumulation | Gradient checkpointing | Attention | Generation batch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| mb2-g16 | 2 / 64 | no | sdpa | 16 |
| mb1-g16 | 1 / 128 | no | sdpa | 16 |
| mb1-gc-g16 | 1 / 128 | yes | sdpa | 16 |
| mb1-gc-eager-g16 | 1 / 128 | yes | eager | 16 |

  All four use max_new_tokens 2048. mb1-g16 and mb1-gc-g16 differ only in gradient checkpointing, which only affects training. Their proofs would very likely repeat each other exactly, so at least one of them is pure waste.

**Where the finding overstates**
- **"A flip is likely" is not backed by the cited evidence.** The q7 file (tmp/kill-test-7b-check/retrieved/q7-1101/tree/cuda-preflight-2/verification.json) shows greedy equal on 3 of 3 prompts (batch 3, 32 tokens, all stopped at eos). Only sampling differed, on 1 of 3. So the waste only happens if a proof fails, and how often that happens is unmeasured.
- **The cost has a ceiling.** orchestrate.py:192-193 waits at most `preflight_wait_s`, which is 9,000 s (probes.py:50). After that, `wait_file` raises (orchestrate.py:90-97) and `after_create` stops the pod (268-279). The price ceiling is `MAX_PRICE` 1.75 (host.py:39). So the waste is at most about 2.5 h, roughly $4 or less. That is close to the reviewer's $3-6, using the brief's 25-60 min per 13B candidate (brief:416). A timeout also replaces the clean `ok: false` with a pre-job failure.
- **The tokenizer_ok half is unlikely to trigger.** The brief's fact sheet gives one chat format for all OLMo-2 sizes (brief:66-75). It is still the same for every candidate, so if it does trigger, continuing is pure waste.
- **olmo2-7b.** Its g16 fallbacks (probes.py:34) are both sdpa. Waste there is about 20-30 min.

**The consequence the reviewer did not raise**
After a proof fails on mb2-g16, mb1-g16 trains differently (accumulation 128 instead of 64). Its slightly different adapter could pass the proof by chance, and the wrapper would choose it (preflight_probe.py:84). Nothing downstream looks at earlier proof failures: orchestrate.py:196 logs only `use_this_recipe`, and nothing under runkit/ mentions batch_proof. This conflicts with lead decision 4 (brief:686): batch 16 is "Allowed only if the preflight proves…", and "Otherwise batch 32 and a longer cap."

**Not a builder deviation from the spec**
The brief's wrapper rule (Item 4.7) names only generation_memory_ok. The gap comes from how decision 4 was added to the spec.

**Fix (as the reviewer proposed)**
- Exit with a verdict right after a failed proof or a failed tokenizer check.
- In the wrapper, after a failed proof skip every later candidate with the same generation batch and attention, and after tokenizer_ok false skip all later candidates.

Severity: should-fix. The fix is cheap, the wasted spend has a ceiling but is real, and the chance-pass path undermines decision 4.

confirmed.title: Reading never ties --manifest to the units, so the bank-scan U can disappear without notice
confirmed.defect: affected_ids() (family_probe_reading.py:204-208) reads whatever file --manifest names, and --manifest is optional (:217, :225). check_pair() (:141-151) compares the two units' job.json manifest_sha256 values with each other but never with the manifest file the reading reads. When the manifest lists no ids, either because the file is the wrong one or because --manifest is missing, bank_scan is None and E_without_affected_pp is left out with no message (:123-125, :180-182).
confirmed.scenario: For olmo2-1b the lead passes --manifest tmp/kt-prepared/prepared-kt-dolly/manifest.json, which is Qwen's manifest with no retokenize receipt and therefore no forbidden_substring_dev_prompt_ids. Leaving --manifest out has the same effect. Either way affected = set(), and the reading prints no bank-scan section and no E without the affected prompts, even though prepared-kt-dolly-olmo2's manifest lists affected dev ids. Brief Item 2b.6 and Item 8 [I-M6] require U with and without those ids. The reverse case can also happen: the llama3 manifest used for an OLMo probe gives a different affected list, because OLMo also forbids '|||'.
confirmed.fix: Make --manifest required, or find the manifest through job.json. Refuse unless sha256 of the manifest bytes equals both units' job.json manifest_sha256. Print bank_scan as 'none listed in the verified manifest' rather than leaving the key out.

I tried to refute this finding and could not. Every part of it holds when I read the code, and I reproduced it on CPU.

**Code reading** (workspace = /Users/spiderishi/Coding/attribution/tmp/claude-workspaces/multi-family-probe-engine-20261007/workspace)
- `--manifest` is optional. scripts/family_probe_reading.py:217 declares it with no `required` and no default.
- When the flag is absent, `affected_ids` returns an empty set (:205-206).
- Otherwise `affected_ids` reads whichever JSON file it is given (:207-208). It never hashes that file.
- `check_pair` (:141-151) compares `recipe_sha256` and `manifest_sha256` only between the two units' `job.json` files. It does this only when both files exist (:147). It never compares them with the `--manifest` file.
- An empty affected set produces `bank_scan: None` (:123). `_shown` then leaves the key out (:164-165), and `reading` leaves out `E_without_affected_pp` (:180-182). Nothing in the output says the scan was skipped or that no manifest was given.

**Why the wrong-manifest scenario is real**
- The Qwen manifest tmp/kt-prepared/prepared-kt-dolly/manifest.json has these `bank_import` keys: files, items, reaudited_items, source_manifest_sha256. It has no `forbidden_substring_dev_prompt_ids`. I checked the keys only.
- That id list is written only on the retokenize path (experiments/safety_selection/prepare_task.py:237-238), and only when the dev count is not zero.
- The OLMo data config forbids `<|im_start|>`, `<|im_end|>`, `<|endoftext|>`, `<|` and `|||`. The Llama config forbids the same list without `|||` (configs/study-kt-data-dolly-olmo2.json:44 and -llama3.json:44). So the reverse case also holds: a Llama manifest can give a smaller affected list for an OLMo probe.

**Why someone would hit it**
- The brief's own command for each probe leaves out `--manifest` (.ai/briefs/multi-family-probe-engine-20261007.md:623).
- The README promises "U without bank-scan ids" and does not say the flag is needed (experiments/safety_selection/README.md:508-512).
- The brief requires "U with and without them" (brief:292 for Item 2b.6 and :605 for Item 8, I-M6).

**Reproduction** (scratchpad/review-mf/manifest-skeptic/repro.py)
I built synthetic unit folders with the test's `folder()` helper. Both units' `job.json` hold `manifest_sha256` = sha256 of an OLMo-like manifest that lists 3 affected ids. I ran `main()` under venv python -B with PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1; no `__pycache__` was created.

| Input | rc | E_without_affected_pp | bank_scan in output | E_pp |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Matching manifest | 0 | 25.38 | yes | 25.0 |
| Qwen-like manifest (hash does not match job.json) | 0 | absent | absent | 25.0 |
| No `--manifest` | 0 | absent | absent | 25.0 |

The run with the wrong manifest was accepted with no error and no message.

**What limits the impact (why minor)**
- `E_without_affected_pp` is a reported sensitivity number. It is not a frozen bar: `bar_checks` (:190-199) and the bars `E_pp` / `E_band` do not use it.
- The docstring does say "with --manifest" (:7, :23).
- Whether OLMo's or Llama's dev bank has any affected ids at all is unknown. The OLMo and Llama sets are not prepared yet: only tmp/kt-prepared/prepared-kt-dolly exists. If the dev count is 0, nothing is lost.

**Fix** (as the reviewer proposed)
- Make `--manifest` required, or find the prepared manifest through `job.json`.

confirmed.title: Two launch.py processes in one kit can create duplicate pods: launch archives create-intent.json, which defeats host.py's intent guard
confirmed.defect: Before each try, launch.py renames create-intent.json (launch.py:131-134). host.py's 'already requested' guard (host.py:112-113) therefore sees nothing, and its name check (host.py:114-118) misses a POST that is still in flight. Inherited from the kill-test kit.
confirmed.scenario: The lead re-runs launch.py olmo2-1b-1101 while the first launcher is still inside create (for example after a terminal disconnect). Both POST pods with the same name. pod.json records one, and the other idles untracked for its 4.5 h cap (about $7).
confirmed.fix: Hold a per-kit flock for launch.py's whole run, and archive the intent only after GET /pods shows no pod with this host's name.

votes.evidence:
I could not refute the mechanism. A forced interleaving reproduces it. The real-world likelihood is lower than the scenario implies.

MECHANISM (confirmed by reading the code):
- Before each try, launch.py renames create-intent.json, create-result.json and timer-settings.json (runkit/family-probe/launch.py:131-134).
- The intent guard in host.py create is therefore empty for a second launcher (host.py:112-113).
- The only remaining dedupe is a GET /pods name match (host.py:114-118). That GET cannot see a POST that is still in flight. The order is: intent saved at :132, POST at :135, pod.json written only at :141.
- The check at host.py:112 and the write at :132 are not atomic in any case.
- grep of the kit for flock, lockf and O_EXCL found nothing.
- The code is inherited unchanged from the kill-test kit (runkit/kill-test-stage0/launch.py:38-40, :47-50; kill-test host.py:101-106). The brief scopes the launch.py changes to the token checks and environment only (brief:514).

REPRODUCTION:
- Setup: byte-identical copies (cmp) of launch.py and host.py in scratchpad/review-mf/skeptic1-intent/, a fake RunPod api, and two threads calling launch.main for olmo2-1b-1101.
- Mode "inflight" (A's POST not yet listed when B's GET runs):
  - POST /pods was called twice with the name 'attribution-probe-olmo2-1b-1101'.
  - pod.json ends as podA, because host.py:141 is a plain overwrite. podB is untracked.
  - Both launchers start 'orchestrate.py after-create' (launch.py:143-147). Two orchestrators then drive the one recorded pod. The reviewer did not mention this second consequence.
- Mode "listed" (A's pod visible to B's GET): B is refused at host.py:117-118, and only one POST is made.
- No file in the workspace was touched, and no __pycache__ was left behind.

WHY THE LIKELIHOOD IS LOW (partial refutation):
- POST timing: in the earlier kits' records (tmp/*/hosts/*/create-intent.json vs create-result.json), all 38 successful creates took 1-2 s from intent to result.
- B's path from the rename to its GET includes a full budget.py run with two network calls (budget.py:66-67) plus a host.py process start. A duplicate therefore needs the two launchers' tries to coincide within about 1-2 s, or needs A's POST to hang toward its 60 s timeout (host.py:68).
- It also needs an operator error: a second launch.py for the same host while the first is alive. If the second starts after pod.json exists, it logs "all hosts created" and exits (launch.py:124-127).
- The "terminal disconnect" framing is weak. A foreground launch.py dies with its host.py child, because run() starts no new session (launch.py:141). A background launcher keeps running, and leads record launcher PIDs (.ai/handoffs/2026-10-06-general-implementation.md:281, 299).

COST:
- The orphan pod is stopped by its in-pod timer at its cap. For this host that is 4.5 h (probes.py:29) at no more than $1.75/h (probe_constants.py MAX_PRICE), so at most about $7.9. An 11 h host (probes.py:50) could cost up to about $19, against a $28.08 balance (brief:596).

- Only the pod.json id is ever stopped (host.py:232-234), so nothing stops the orphan before its cap.

- A whole-kit flock held for the whole 2 h run would also block launching other hosts of the same kit. A per-host lock (for example on hosts/HOST/launch.lock), held across rename, budget check, create and popen, is enough.
- "Archive only after GET shows no pod" alone does not close the in-flight window.
- Also: start orchestrate only when host.py create exits 0. launch.py:143 checks only that pod.json exists.

SEPARATE LIMIT (not a duplicate): with a single launcher, if a POST times out on the client side after RunPod created the pod, the pod is never tracked. Only HTTPError is caught (host.py:71). The next try archives the intent, and the name check then refuses every retry, so the pod idles until its cap.

Verdict: real, minor.

I could not refute it. I reproduced it on CPU with fakes.

How the code allows it:
- launch.py:131-134 renames create-intent.json, create-result.json and timer-settings.json before every try. It does not check whether another process is still inside create, and the kit has no lock: launch.py:1-160 has no flock, fcntl or pid file.
- host.py:112-113 refuses only when pod.json or create-intent.json exists.
- host.py:114-118 refuses only when GET /pods already lists a pod with the same name.
- host.py:132 writes the intent before the POST. host.py:135 sends the POST. pod.json is written only after it returns (host.py:141).
- So a second launcher B can slip through. B's rename has to fall after A's intent write (host.py:132). B's GET /pods (host.py:114) then has to run before A's pod is listed. B passes both guards and sends a second POST with the same name_of(host) (host.py:95-99).
- The logic is inherited unchanged. The kill-test kit has the same rename at runkit/kill-test-stage0/launch.py:38 and the same guards at runkit/kill-test-stage0/host.py:101-107.

Reproduction:
- I copied the kit to scratchpad/review-mf/kit and added a fake plan.json and ssh/key.pub. Script: scratchpad/review-mf/race.py.
- The fake api() makes POST /pods take 1 s and lists a pod only after its POST returns. Thread A runs host.create. Once A's create-intent.json exists, launch.main(["h1"]) runs as launcher B.
- Result: 2 POSTs, both named attribution-probe-h1. pod.json ends up holding pod2, so pod1 is untracked. A's intent and timer settings were renamed "-failed-". B also spawned orchestrate after-create.
- I ran no network calls, and no __pycache__ was left.

Effects the reviewer did not mention:
- launch.py:143 checks only that pod.json exists, not that this process created it. Both launchers therefore start a detached orchestrate.py after-create (launch.py:145-147) for the same host. That means two orchestrators, possibly on different pods, because host.py state() at host.py:102-106 checks only the shared name.
- B's budget check (launch.py:136) ran before A's pod existed, so the $6 reserve rule can be broken. For the 11 h probe (probes.py:50), two pods could commit 2 x $19.25 against the roughly $28 balance (brief:596).

What limits it (why minor, not should-fix):
- It needs an operator error: two launchers for the same host in the same kit. Nothing in the kit, README or brief tells anyone to do that. Past runs started one nohup launcher per host, and handoffs record the launcher PIDs (.ai/handoffs/2026-10-06-general-implementation.md:281,299).
- The timing must line up. B's rename, then its budget.py subprocess (two HTTP calls), then its host.py GET must all land inside A's single successful POST. That is a few seconds out of rounds that are 300 s or more apart (launch.py:26,155).
- The untracked pod still has its in-pod stop timer (host.py:119-131), so the loss is bounded: up to 4.5 h x $1.75, about $7.9, for olmo2-1b (probes.py:29). budget.py:56-62 counts a running pod with no recorded cap at 11 h, so later launches stay conservative.
- A single launcher retrying after a failed or timed-out POST is still protected by the name check at host.py:117.

Note on the suggested fix:
- The proposed "archive the intent only after GET /pods shows no pod with this name" does not close the race by itself, because an in-flight POST is not listed yet.
- A per-kit (or per-host) flock held for the whole run of launch.py is the real fix.
- launch.py:143 should also start orchestrate only when its own host.py create returned 0.

confirmed.title: Second-judge summary is not tied to the probe; all five probes and the Qwen-7B check use the same unit keys
